summary:
Answer: yes, our rules can run on analog in-memory (AIMC) crossbar simulators, but no single maintained tool gives both device-level learning physics for a custom rule and calibrated costs on this Windows PC. The tools split three ways.

(a) Learning physics without costs:
- aihwkit (Linux only) is the reference. tile.update(x, d) applies any outer-product rule (Hebbian, node perturbation (NP), DFA) through stochastic pulse trains with asymmetry, bounds and variation.
- Per-device max_bound/min_bound can force synapses off.
- It counts pulses (GPU builds only) but has no energy, latency or area model.
- XBTorch (2026, arXiv 2601.07086) and CrossSim v2.0 (2023, legacy) are alternatives.

(b) Costs without learning: CrossSim v3 (no energy and no training), NeuroSim V1.4/V1.5, MNSIM 2.0, CiMLoop (deprecated June 2026) and its successor AccelForge/HWComponents, and ZigZag.

(c) Both, built in: only the NeuroSim training versions.
- MLP+NeuroSim V3.0 is C++; it reports read and write energy, latency and pulse counts; and a custom rule or pruning mask is a short edit in Train.cpp.
- DNN+NeuroSim V2.1 is Linux/CUDA, assumes a BP dataflow, and is CNN-scale.
- aihwkit-lightning, MemTorch and MemIntelli are rejected: none of them models in-situ weight updates.

This PC: MSYS2 g++ 11.2 with OpenMP, make and cmake are present, so MLP+NeuroSim should compile natively (inferred, untested). MSVC is absent, which blocks a Windows aihwkit build and XBTorch's qtorch compile at import. The docker CLI is not usable. aihwkit, DNN+NeuroSim V2.1, NeuroSim V1.5 and AccelForge need RunPod.

Already done:
- BP vs DFA was compared on CIM with DNN+NeuroSim (arXiv 2212.14337): BP keeps the accuracy lead under hardware imperfections; DFA buys parallel speed.
- Spiking DFA on RRAM IMC: 1.37-2.1x energy reduction vs PipeLayer (2507.15603).
- Zeroth-order training on IMC is costed as read-modify-write overhead; an implicit perturbation unit cuts it to 0.46-0.83x (2608.21223).
- Perturbative MGD (2303.03986, 2501.15403).
- Sparse stochastic updates cut weight-update pulses by 90% in an MLP (1906.02393).
- Crossbar-aware pruning for on-chip ReRAM training (2111.09272).
- In-situ pruning during training on a fabricated RRAM CIM chip (2506.13151).
- Selective update (doi 10.1002/aisy.202500150).
- Analog-weight reprogramming cost avoided via LoRA in SRAM (2601.10037).
- Plain analog SGD has an error floor on asymmetric devices; Tiki-Taka (c-TTv2/AGAD) fixes it (2406.12774; doi 10.1038/s41467-024-51221-z). These are the honest BP baselines on AIMC.
- Synapses whose eligibility trace is stored as local temperature (2411.18272), a physical 'medium' close to our principle.

Best honest-positive bet for this family: the subtractive/write-budget angle at MLP scale, where hub allocation worked.
- On AIMC, writes cost energy and endurance per pulse. A pruned device is never written, and removing whole rows, columns or tiles also saves ADC and driver energy.
- Stage A, Windows now: MLP+NeuroSim with dense BP, learning-time gradual pruning, hub budgets, and NP/DFA/Hebbian variants. Measure accuracy against modelled read and write energy and pulses.
- Stage B, RunPod (needs the user's OK): aihwkit GPU with ReRAM/ECRAM presets and pulse counters. Baselines: c-TTv2/AGAD and sparse-update methods. Pulse and MVM counts can be priced with NeuroSim or HWComponents energies.
- Guard against 'saving by construction': compare at iso-accuracy and report structured savings.
- Local rule beating BP on energy is unlikely. By my reasoning, NP costs about two forward MVMs plus a rank-1 update per step versus forward, backward and update for BP, and NP needs more steps.
- A testable hypothesis: device update asymmetry may supply the decay that NP needed as explicit weight decay on GPU.

All energies from these tools are model-based estimates.

scout.name: IBM aihwkit (Analog Hardware Acceleration Kit)
scout.family: Analog in-memory computing, resistive crossbar (PCM / ReRAM / ECRAM / capacitor cells). Device-level functional simulator: PyTorch layers on top of a C++/CUDA engine (RPUCuda)
scout.what_it_models: Analog tiles with forward and backward MVM non-idealities: DAC/ADC quantization and bounds, output-referred noise, weight noise, IR drop (including a time-stepped IR-drop inference tile), PCM drift, programming noise. The pulsed-update model applies stochastic row/column pulse trains with a finite step per coincidence (dw_min), up/down asymmetry, soft or hard bounds, device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variation, decay/diffusion, and corrupt (stuck) devices. Device families: ConstantStep, LinearStep, SoftBounds, PowStep and others, plus compound devices (vector unit cell, transfer/Tiki-Taka, mixed precision). Tile size is configurable, and TileModuleArray splits large matrices across tiles. Dynamic input scaling, bound management and update management are included.
scout.learning_support: Yes, in-situ. Built-in: analog SGD with stochastic pulse trains, mixed precision (digital rank update plus transfer), Tiki-Taka v1, TTv2, c-TTv2 and AGAD (Nature Comms 2024, doi 10.1038/s41467-024-51221-z), and a CustomTile for prototyping algorithms in floating point. Custom local rules: the low-level tile.update(x_input, d_input) applies W -= lr * d^T x through the pulsed device model (verified in tiles/periphery.py). So any rule that is a (batched) outer product of a pre- and a post-synaptic vector keeps the full device effects: Hebbian (d = -y), node perturbation (d proportional to dL*xi/sigma^2), DFA (d = (B e) * f'). Full-matrix weight perturbation does not fit the parallel rank-1 update. Forcing devices off: per-device hidden parameters (verified names in rpu_pulsed_device.cpp: max_bound, min_bound, dwmin_up, dwmin_down, ...) can be written with set_hidden_parameters. There is also a random corrupt_devices_prob option (sets min bound = max bound). Targeted per-synapse masks are not a built-in feature (my reading of the code).
scout.cost_model: No energy, latency or area model. Optional pulse counters (count_pulses, read with tile.get_pulse_counters()); the docstring says 'Only for GPU devices currently implemented'. Any energy figure has to be computed outside the tool, e.g. pulse counts and MVM/ADC counts multiplied by NeuroSim or HWComponents per-operation energies.
scout.calibration: PCM inference model calibrated on measurements from a 1-million-device PCM chip (README). Training presets (e.g. ReRamArrayOMPresetDevice, ReRamArrayHfO2PresetDevice, ReRAM ES/SB, ECRAM, capacitor) are fitted to measured devices or literature models. v1.0.0 adds a CMO/HfOx ReRAM inference noise model. No cost calibration, because there is no cost model.
scout.last_release_or_commit: PyPI 1.1.0 uploaded 2026-02-10 (GitHub release 2026-02-03). Repo commit 'Release/aihwkit 1.2.0 (#818)' on 2026-10-07; VERSION.txt on master reads 1.2.0, not yet on PyPI.
scout.windows_native: No. PyPI has never shipped a win_amd64 wheel (1.1.0: manylinux_2_27/2_28 cp310-312 and macOS arm64 only). conda-forge aihwkit and aihwkit-gpu are linux-64 only, and the docs say conda works on 'Linux or WSL'. A source build needs a torch-ABI C++ toolchain (MSVC on Windows), OpenBLAS/MKL, cmake >= 4.2.1 and pybind11 (plus CUDA for GPU), and the developer-install doc targets Linux. MSVC (cl.exe) is not on PATH on this PC.
scout.gpu: CUDA through the compiled RPUCuda engine. The PyPI 1.1.0 wheels are CPU-only and require torch >= 2.9.1. GPU builds come from IBM-hosted manylinux wheels (aihwkit-1.1.0 cp310/311/312) or conda-forge aihwkit-gpu (cuda-version >= 12.9, < 13). The extension is compiled against a specific torch ABI, so do not pair it with an arbitrary torch 2.11. Master adds builds for torch >= 2.14 (C++20). An AMD ROCm fork exists.
scout.install_route_this_pc: RunPod Linux A40 (sm_86): conda-forge aihwkit-gpu (resolves a matching pytorch and CUDA >= 12.9), or the IBM GPU wheel with matching torch. The CPU wheel is enough for small-MLP pulsed training, but pulse counters work only on GPU. Not runnable on this Windows PC without WSL.
scout.notes: Best device-physics testbed for local rules. Papers: AICAS 2021 doi 10.1109/aicas51828.2021.9458494 (arXiv 2104.02184); tutorial arXiv 2307.09357 (APL ML doi 10.1063/5.0168089). The honest BP baseline on AIMC is c-TTv2/AGAD, not plain analog SGD: arXiv 2406.12774 proves an asymptotic error floor for plain SGD on asymmetric devices, while Tiki-Taka converges exactly. The docs say Tiki-Taka uses device asymmetry to implicitly decay its fast array. My hypothesis: asymmetric (SoftBounds) devices might supply the stabilising decay that node perturbation needed as explicit weight decay 5e-4 on GPU. Testable here. CustomTile updates in floating point and has no device physics, so use AnalogTile.update for physics.

scout.name: IBM aihwkit-lightning
scout.family: AIMC hardware-aware training for inference: pure PyTorch, optional Triton kernels
scout.what_it_models: Inference non-idealities injected during training: weight-noise and output-noise injection, input/output (DAC/ADC) quantization, weight clipping/modification, tiling along the input dimension. Models export to aihwkit.
scout.learning_support: No in-situ or pulsed learning. Weights are ordinary digital tensors trained by any torch optimizer; AnalogOptimizer only adds post-step clipping. A custom rule can update the weights, but there is no device-update physics and no write cost, so it is not a fair AIMC learning testbed.
scout.cost_model: None
scout.calibration: Noise settings mirror aihwkit inference configs. No update-device calibration.
scout.last_release_or_commit: PyPI 2.1.0 on 2026-09-15 (GitHub v2.1.0 same day). Last commit 2026-10-05.
scout.windows_native: Installable (py3-none-any wheel), but 2.1.0 pins torch==2.13.0 ('PyTorch 2.14 introduced C++ header changes that break the build'). That conflicts with the venv's torch 2.11, so --no-deps would be needed (untested). Triton mode is off by default.
scout.gpu: CUDA through torch. Triton kernels need compute capability >= 7.0 and are optional.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Separate Windows env with --no-deps, or RunPod. Only worth it to check inference robustness of pruned nets.
scout.notes: Rejected for learning experiments: it has no update physics and no costs. Paper: NeurIPS 2024 workshop (openreview QNdxOgGmhR, linked from PyPI).

scout.name: Sandia CrossSim v3.x (current)
scout.family: AIMC accuracy simulator: NumPy/CuPy core with Torch and Keras layer wrappers
scout.what_it_models: Programming errors, conductance drift, cycle-to-cycle read noise (lumped-noise fast path added in 3.2.1), ADC/DAC models including circuit-based ADCs, parasitic metal resistance via an internal circuit solver (new Array interface in 3.1.1), errors from nonlinear I-V (3.2.0), bit slicing, negative-number schemes, array size. Custom device models (e.g. RRAM_Wan added in 3.1). Torch RNN/LSTM/GRU layers since 3.2.0. The IISWC2026 tutorial adds an SNN notebook.
scout.learning_support: No in-situ training. The 3.0 notes say 'Neural network training and outer product update support removed'. The Torch interface (3.1+) supports hardware-aware training only, i.e. backprop through a noisy analog forward. A custom local rule would have to compute dW digitally and reprogram (programming-error model), not apply pulse-level updates.
scout.cost_model: None. Official site: CrossSim 'does not explicitly model the energy, area, or speed of analog accelerators'.
scout.calibration: Device error models parameterised from published/measured devices (not checked in detail).
scout.last_release_or_commit: Release 3.2.1 on 2026-06-03 (3.2.0 on 2026-04-03). Last commit 2026-09-27 (IISWC2026 tutorial: Basics, Codesign, Models, HardwareAwareTraining, SNNs).
scout.windows_native: Yes. Pure Python (numpy, scipy). The GitHub page says tested on Ubuntu 18.04 and Windows 10 with Python 3.11.6 and PyTorch 2.2.1. Not on PyPI; install from a git clone.
scout.gpu: Optional CuPy (tested CuPy 12.3 with CUDA 12.3). No torch pin.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Windows venv, pip install from a clone. Useful only for inference-robustness checks (parasitics, ADC) of pruned or hub-allocated nets.
scout.notes: Rejected for in-situ learning: no update physics and no cost model.

scout.name: Sandia CrossSim v2.0 (legacy, last version with training)
scout.family: AIMC accuracy simulator with a training mode
scout.what_it_models: The v3 non-idealities (older implementation), plus training-time conductance updates from lookup tables generated from experimental data. These capture write nonlinearity, write asymmetry, write stochasticity and device-to-device variability.
scout.learning_support: In-situ training with outer-product updates through LUT device models. A custom rule would replace the outer-product update; this is DIY and the primitive was removed in 3.0.
scout.cost_model: None (same disclaimer as v3).
scout.calibration: Device LUTs derived from experimental device data, shipped in the cross-sim-data submodule (about 1.2 GB together with models).
scout.last_release_or_commit: 2.0 released 2023-10-06. Release note: 'Training support will be removed from subsequent releases until a long-term feature maintainer can be found'.
scout.windows_native: Tested on Windows 10, but with a legacy stack: Python 3.7.6, TensorFlow 2.4.1, CuPy 8.3/10.3.1. It cannot share the project venv.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Separate legacy Python 3.7 env on Windows (untested). Low priority, unmaintained.
scout.notes: The only lookup-table update model among the tools checked. Prior use: arXiv 2304.11337 trained a DNN inside CrossSim (2023).

scout.name: MLP+NeuroSim V3.0 (Georgia Tech NeuroSim, on-chip learning version)
scout.family: CIM device-circuit-algorithm co-simulator with built-in on-chip training. C++ only.
scout.what_it_models: Two-layer MLP (default 400-100-10, MNIST; 8000 images per epoch, 125 epochs) on synaptic arrays. Cell types: analog eNVM RealDevice (LTP/LTD nonlinearity, conductance range and levels, cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variation), MeasuredDevice (measured LTP/LTD curves), IdealDevice, digital eNVM (e.g. STT-MRAM with parallel read-out), SRAM, hybrid cells (3T1C+NVM, 2T1F FeFET). 1T1R or cross-point arrays. Periphery from technology files, with FinFET (<20 nm) calibration added in 2020.
scout.learning_support: On-chip training is built in: backprop with SGD, momentum, Adagrad, RMSprop or Adam (Train.cpp). Every update goes through WriteCell with per-device pulse counts, nonlinearity and variation. Custom rule: replace the delta computation (s1/s2 around Train.cpp lines 507-520) and gradt = s1*Input (around line 566) with Hebbian, node-perturbation or DFA terms. Pruning: skip WriteCell for masked synapses and hold them at minimum conductance; their write energy is then zero in the model.
scout.cost_model: Per epoch. Read energy: array wire caps, cell currents I*V*t, and subarray periphery (read circuits, adders, muxes, decoders, DFFs). Write energy: per-pulse V^2*G*t, half-selected cells, FeFET gate caps. Write latency for LTP and LTD, area, leakage. Running totals totalNumPulse and totalWeightUpdate.
scout.calibration: NeuroSim circuit models with FinFET calibration. The silicon-validation papers (Frontiers AI 2021, doi 10.3389/frai.2021.659060; 40 nm RRAM CIM macro, AICAS 2021, doi 10.1109/aicas51828.2021.9458501) concern the DNN+NeuroSim line, not this exact version. Device presets come from literature and measured curves.
scout.last_release_or_commit: Standalone repo last commit 2021-11-03. Also branch MLPInferenceV3.0 in neurosim/NeuroSim (updated 2025-01-01); the monorepo README calls it 'MLP Inference' although the code trains on-chip.
scout.windows_native: Likely, but untested. The makefile is plain 'g++ -fopenmp -O3 -std=c++0x', and the top-level sources include no Linux-only headers. MSYS2 g++ 11.2 with working -fopenmp, make and cmake are already on this PC. 'make run' uses stdbuf/tee, so call the binary directly.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Windows native through MSYS2, using only what is already installed. This is the fastest route to a write-plus-read energy scoreboard for MLP-scale rules. RunPod also works.
scout.notes: The only tool runnable on this PC now that couples learning dynamics with device-update non-idealities and a write-plus-read energy model for a custom rule. The MLP scale matches where hub allocation worked on GPU. Limits: tiny sigmoid MLP, old technology models, NC licence. Citation required: NeuroSim+ IEDM 2017 and the ICONS 2019 V3.0 paper. Do not 'pip install neurosim': that PyPI name is an unrelated BCI reinforcement-learning gym (0.1.0, 2026-02-25).

scout.name: DNN+NeuroSim V2.1 (on-chip training)
scout.family: CIM benchmarking framework for on-chip training: PyTorch wrapper plus the NeuroSim C++ core
scout.what_it_models: VGG-8 on CIFAR-10 by default, with WAGE-quantised training and one cell per synapse. Update non-idealities applied in train.py: LTP/LTD nonlinearity, device-to-device and cycle-to-cycle variation; FeFET polarisation during update. Read-out with a multi-level sense amp (CSA or VSA) or a SAR ADC. FinFET-calibrated technology. Chip/tile/PE/subarray hierarchy driven by real training traces.
scout.learning_support: Built-in on-chip training is BP with WAGE and momentum. Device effects are applied to param.grad by wage_quantizer.QG/W. Custom rule: write the rule's dW into param.grad before QG to keep the device effects. The cost path assumes the BP dataflow and charges activation-gradient (backward MVM) energy, so rules without a backward pass need C++ edits. Precedent: arXiv 2212.14337 compared DFA with BP using DNN+NeuroSim.
scout.cost_model: Per epoch: latency and energy split into forward, activation gradient, weight gradient and weight update (plus peaks), area, leakage, and per-epoch breakdown CSVs. Includes ADC/sense-amp, buffers and interconnect.
scout.calibration: NeuroSim silicon validation (V1.3 line; Frontiers AI 2021 doi 10.3389/frai.2021.659060) and FinFET calibration.
scout.last_release_or_commit: Repo last commit 2024-02-21 ('fixes for numpy compatibility'); PyTorch 2.0/GCC update 2023-04-22. Branch 2DTrainingV2.1 in the NeuroSim monorepo dated 2025-01-01. TCAD paper doi 10.1109/TCAD.2020.3043731.
scout.windows_native: No. Install steps are Linux (make). The Python wrapper hard-codes .cuda() and drives the C++ core through a generated shell trace script. README warns of about 12 h for VGG-8 over 256 epochs.
scout.gpu: CUDA needed by the wrapper; the C++ core runs on CPU.
scout.install_route_this_pc: RunPod Linux only.
scout.notes: CNN scale, which is where hub allocation failed on GPU. Use only if the MLP results justify scaling up.

scout.name: NeuroSim V1.4 / V1.5-dev (DNN+NeuroSim inference, incl. digital CIM and systolic variants)
scout.family: CIM performance/power/area plus accuracy, inference only (analog and digital CIM, SRAM and eNVM)
scout.what_it_models: V1.4: 130 nm to 1 nm nodes (FinFET, GAA nanosheet), partial-parallel read, XY-bus or H-tree interconnect; separate digital-CIM and digital-systolic branches. V1.5 (TCAD 2026, doi 10.1109/tcad.2026.3674448; arXiv 2505.02314): TensorRT post-training-quantisation flow including ViTs, statistical noise injection from SPICE or silicon data, capacitive NVM, and up to 6.5x faster runtime.
scout.learning_support: None (inference).
scout.cost_model: Area, latency, energy and leakage, including ADC, periphery, buffers and interconnect.
scout.calibration: Validated against silicon since V1.3; FinFET/GAA technology libraries.
scout.last_release_or_commit: V1.4 repo commit 2025-03-09. Monorepo branch 2DInferenceV1.4 updated 2025-10-26; 2DInferenceV1.5-dev updated 2026-07-18; main README 2026-01-16.
scout.windows_native: No. Tested on RHEL 8.8 and Ubuntu 20.04 with gcc and CUDA 12.
scout.install_route_this_pc: RunPod, and only if inference PPA of a pruned network is needed.
scout.notes: Rejected for learning. Same PyPI 'neurosim' name trap as above.

scout.name: MNSIM 2.0 (Tsinghua)
scout.family: Processing-in-memory behaviour-level modelling tool: Python and PyTorch
scout.what_it_models: Inference on memristor PIM architectures: latency, area, power and energy, plus accuracy under stuck-at faults, device variation, R-ratio and quantisation. Tile-connection-graph mapping; hardware described in SimConfig.ini.
scout.learning_support: None. Pre-trained weights are only mapped. A training-in-memory variant, MNSIM-TIME (AICAS 2021, doi 10.1109/aicas51828.2021.9458441), exists as a paper; no public code was found under the guessed thu-nics repo names.
scout.cost_model: Yes, for inference only (behaviour-level models).
scout.license: No LICENSE file at the repo root (404), so reuse is legally unclear.
scout.windows_native: Probably (pure Python plus torch); untested.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Not recommended.
scout.notes: Rejected: inference only, and the licence is unclear.

scout.name: MemTorch
scout.family: Memristive deep-learning simulator: PyTorch with a C++/CUDA extension
scout.what_it_models: Converts trained networks to memristive crossbars. Device models and non-idealities (finite states, faults, endurance/retention, nonlinear I-V), 1T1R or 1R, tile_shape, ADC_resolution, max_input_voltage, programming routines including passive-crossbar programming.
scout.learning_support: No in-situ training. patch_model converts pre-trained models, and the docs mention no training, backward pass or update.
scout.cost_model: None found in the README or the docs pages checked.
scout.calibration: Device-model parameters from literature; not verified.
scout.last_release_or_commit: Release 1.1.6 on 2022-02-25; last commit 2022-04-13. arXiv 2004.10971; Neurocomputing doi 10.1016/j.neucom.2022.02.043.
scout.windows_native: memtorch-cpu win_amd64 wheels exist only for cp37-cp39, none for cp310. A source build needs MSVC, plus CUDA 10.1 for GPU.
scout.gpu: Old CUDA extension; likely incompatible with torch 2.11.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Rejected.
scout.notes: Unmaintained since 2022 and inference only.

scout.name: CiMLoop (Timeloop+Accelergy v4), deprecated
scout.family: Full-stack compute-in-memory cost model (energy/area/latency)
scout.what_it_models: User-defined CiM circuits, architecture, workload and mapping, with a statistical energy model that depends on data values. Includes a model of the Albireo photonic accelerator.
scout.learning_support: None. It has no accuracy or learning model.
scout.cost_model: Energy, area and latency with ADC/DAC and periphery, mapping-aware.
scout.calibration: The paper claims accuracy against published CiM macros; the numbers were not checked.
scout.last_release_or_commit: Last commit 2026-07-09. README carries a 'no longer maintained' warning (commit 2026-06-22) pointing to AccelForge and HWComponents. Paper: ISPASS 2024, doi 10.1109/ispass61541.2024.00012, arXiv 2405.07259.
scout.windows_native: No. Distributed as Docker compose, and no docker CLI is on PATH on this PC (Docker Desktop files exist but are unusable as-is).
scout.install_route_this_pc: Use AccelForge instead.
scout.notes: Rejected: deprecated, and cost-only.

scout.name: AccelForge + HWComponents (+ hwcomponents-neurosim / -library / -adc / -cacti)
scout.family: Accelerator modelling and mapping framework, successor of Timeloop/Accelergy/CiMLoop. Cost model only.
scout.what_it_models: Composable device, circuit and architecture models with fast mappers. HWComponents provides area, energy, latency and leakage models. hwcomponents-neurosim compiles the NeuroSim V1.3 C++ core to model CiM row/column drivers, flash ADC, memory cells (NVMExplorer/NVSim cell files), and voltage or temporal DACs. The library includes components taken from published chips (commits 'Jia components', 'Neurram components').
scout.learning_support: None built in. A training step could be written as Einsums and costed: the hwcomponents-neurosim components expose write/update actions that return NeuroSim 'Write Energy'. This is DIY, with no device-update dynamics and no accuracy.
scout.cost_model: Area, energy, latency/throughput and leakage, with mapping optimisation.
scout.calibration: Component models from NeuroSim, CACTI and published chips.
scout.license: MIT, but hwcomponents-neurosim bundles NeuroSim V1.3 (CC BY-NC) as a git submodule.
scout.last_release_or_commit: accelforge 1.0.467 on PyPI (2026-07-14), repo commits up to 2026-10-05. hwcomponents 1.0.114 (2026-06-22); hwcomponents-neurosim 1.0.43 (2026-06-20). Paper: arXiv 2609.11906 (2026-09-10).
scout.windows_native: No. hwcomponents packages require Python >= 3.12. islpy-barvinok has no Windows wheels. hwcomponents-neurosim wheels are manylinux and macOS only; the sdist runs make to compile NeuroSim.
scout.install_route_this_pc: RunPod, Python 3.12 env, as an optional independent cost back-end that turns MVM, ADC and write counts into energy.
scout.notes: Cost-only. Complements aihwkit, which has learning physics but no costs.

scout.name: XBTorch (GWU / Western Digital / ARL, 2026)
scout.family: Crossbar DNN simulator, PyTorch-native
scout.what_it_models: Analytical device models (cycle-to-cycle, device-to-device, nonlinearity) and tabular jump/lookup-table models for ReRAM, FeFET, PCM and MTJ. Custom devices from measured dG-per-pulse data via Kriging (smt). ADC/DAC precision, stuck-at faults, device retention (added 2026-07), WAGE quantisation, gradient decomposition (SBPCA, NMF, SVD), LLM evaluation through lm-eval.
scout.learning_support: Weight updates go through device models: gradient is turned into integer pulses by stochastic rounding (p = round(p_max * dL)), then applied by the device model. It wraps PyTorch optimizers, so a custom rule written into .grad keeps the device effects. The paper frames gradient compression as 'fewer device writes'. There is no stochastic pulse-coincidence (parallel outer-product) model.
scout.cost_model: None. The paper says XBTorch 'intentionally trades detailed system-level performance estimation'.
scout.calibration: Presets: NeuroSim real/ideal ReRAM, and lookup-table ReRAM and FeFET from prior works.
scout.license: BSD-3 per README/LICENSE; the pyproject classifier says MIT (inconsistent).
scout.last_release_or_commit: Last commit 2026-07-18. pyproject version 1.0.0; not on PyPI (404). arXiv 2601.07086 (2026-01-11).
scout.windows_native: Conditional. The package is pure Python, but 'import xbtorch' imports qtorch.quant, which JIT-compiles C++ (and CUDA when available) extensions at import via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load. That needs MSVC Build Tools, which are not present here.
scout.gpu: torch >= 2.3, so 2.11 is fine. qtorch compiles a CUDA extension when CUDA is available.
scout.install_route_this_pc: RunPod Linux (gcc), or install MSVC Build Tools on Windows (needs the user's OK).
scout.notes: The newest (2026) training-capable crossbar simulator found. A lighter Python alternative to aihwkit for custom-rule device updates, but it has no cost model.

scout.name: MemIntelli (HUST, 2025)
scout.family: Memristive IMC simulator: PyTorch and NumPy
scout.what_it_models: Bit-sliced, variable-precision (INT/FP) MVM on memristive arrays: high/low conductance states, write variation, stuck-at-high/low rates, read variation, voltage noise, DAC/ADC resolution, number of conductance levels, array partitioning.
scout.learning_support: Hardware-aware, limited-precision training (LeNet-5 on MNIST in the paper) through noisy MVMs. No pulse-level update model.
scout.cost_model: None (accuracy and SNR only).
scout.calibration: Equivalent-circuit math abstractions; not described as calibrated.
scout.license: PyPI says MIT, but the README says 'publicly available on a non-commercial basis' (inconsistent).
scout.windows_native: Probably (pure Python); requires numpy < 2.
scout.gpu: torch CUDA. The paper reports ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 at 0.27 img/s on CPU vs 7 img/s on GPU.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Not recommended.
scout.notes: Rejected: no in-situ update physics and no cost model.

scout.name: NeuroPack (2022) / PyT-NeuroPack (2024)
scout.family: Algorithm-level memristor neuromorphic (SNN) simulator: Python, runs as an ArC One plugin
scout.what_it_models: Empirical metal-oxide memristor model (Messaris 2017) fitted to measured devices. LIF, Izhikevich and Tempotron neurons. Fully connected layers only; PyT-NeuroPack adds a PyTorch convolutional front-end.
scout.learning_support: Online learning rules: STDP, surrogate-gradient BP, Tempotron, DRTP. Custom rules go in NeuroCores/core_X.py.
scout.cost_model: Tracks write pulse voltage and duration; no energy model reported.
scout.calibration: Memristor parameters extracted from measured devices.
scout.license: A licence file was added in 2022 (type not checked).
scout.last_release_or_commit: NeuroPack last commit 2022-04-24. Frontiers in Nanotechnology 2022, doi 10.3389/fnano.2022.851856. PyT-NeuroPack: NEWCAS 2024, doi 10.1109/newcas58973.2024.10666111 (code not checked).
scout.windows_native: Yes. It runs inside the ArC One GUI (VirtualArC) on Windows.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Possible on Windows, but GUI-driven, fully-connected only and unmaintained. Low priority, and closer to the neuromorphic scout's scope.
scout.notes: The only tool checked with ready-made local and three-factor-style rules on memristors, but it is SNN-oriented and has no cost model.

summary:
Scope: neuromorphic SDKs/emulators and hardware-agnostic cost metrics. Analog in-memory computing, physical-learning and photonic tools belong to other scouts; only the overlaps are noted here.

1) Verdict. No open, Windows-native tool gives a calibrated cost for learning while inferring on a non-von-Neumann chip. The tools fall into four groups:
- Calibrated inference-cost simulator. SANA-FE (pip wheel cp310 win_amd64) has per-event energy and latency. Its Loihi-1 preset predicts measured Loihi energy within 12% and latency within 25% on 3 applications (IEEE TCAD 2025). It has no learning or plasticity unit.
- Bit-accurate rule emulators with no cost model. Lava's CPU Loihi2SimCfg supports Loihi 2-factor and 3-factor learning-rule strings (dw/dd/dt over traces, 8-bit weights). All Lava repos were archived (README change 2026-05-13); the last release is 0.10.0 with Python 3.10 and numpy<2 pins. Brian2Loihi covers Loihi 1 but has been stale since 2021.
- Counters only. NeuroBench, the Sinabs and Norse synops counters, and syops count operations. They count no weight updates and no memory traffic.
- Real hardware with measured power, open free to individuals. Only EBRAINS offers this:
  - BrainScaleS-2: analog, 6-bit weights stored per synapse, local rules and structural plasticity programmable as C++ on the on-chip plasticity processors (PPU), no local install.
  - SpiNNaker 1 via sPyNNaker: STDP, neuromodulation and structural plasticity.
- Closed or unsuitable:
  - Loihi 2: INRC membership is for research groups, and the SDK is archived.
  - SpiNNaker2: needs private repos plus hardware access; the py-spinnaker2 docs say 'on-chip learning isn't supported yet'.
  - Akida: on-chip learning only in the last layer, 1-bit; power is measured only on a device.
  - Xylo and Speck: no on-chip learning; samna runs on Linux and macOS only.
  - NengoLoihi: Loihi 1 only, stale.

2) Prior art already overlapping the thesis:
- DEEP R prune-and-regrow training within 64 KB per core on a SpiNNaker 2 prototype: 1.3% of connections active, 96.6% on MNIST, about 100x less power and energy than an x86 CPU (doi 10.3389/fnins.2018.00840).
- Reward-based structural plasticity on the same prototype (arXiv 1903.08500).
- Constant-fan-in structural plasticity on BrainScaleS-2 (arXiv 1912.12047; 92.3% on Iris).
- Rewiring plus STDP on SpiNNaker (10.3389/fnins.2018.00434).
- GeNN GPU structural plasticity (arXiv 2510.19764): sparse e-prop plus DEEP R trains up to 10x faster than dense baselines.
- CLP-SNN on Loihi 2 (arXiv 2511.01553): a 3-factor local rule for online continual learning. It used 0.05 mJ against 333 mJ for a Jetson Orin Nano, which splits into about 22.6x from the algorithm and about 295x from the hardware. However, it relies on a frozen EfficientNet-B0 feature extractor running on a GPU, and host I/O is excluded. CLANE (arXiv 2605.28387) extends it.
- EventProp backprop running on SpiNNaker2 (arXiv 2412.15021).
- Cost-model warnings: Dampfhoffer 2023 finds SNNs win only at 0.15 to 1.38 spikes per synapse per inference once memory access is counted. SATA (arXiv 2204.05422) finds SNN BPTT costs 1.27x an ANN on a systolic accelerator.

3) Best chance of an honest positive result. This is my inference and is untested.
- The task: online class-incremental learning in which learning is an event-gated local 2- or 3-factor update on a readout or prototype layer.
- A hard per-neuron synapse budget, with the hub-allocation rule as the budget. This is comparable to the constant fan-in on BrainScaleS-2 and Akida's num_weights.
- One declared cost model for both contenders, reported as an estimate:
  - The neuromorphic side prices synaptic events, spike messages and weight updates. Use the SANA-FE Loihi preset plus an explicitly stated per-update cost, because no calibrated learning-energy number was found.
  - The backprop side is priced with a GPU or systolic-accelerator model in the style of SATA.
- Local stack:
  - Main venv plus neurobench for counts, and sanafe for energy.
  - A separate Python 3.10 venv with lava-nc 0.10.0, to check that each rule fits Loihi's learning engine.
  - Then confirm on EBRAINS BrainScaleS-2, which is free, to get measured chip power. That is a measurement on neuromorphic hardware, not on a GPU, so the project rule needs an explicit decision.
- RunPod is not needed for this family. It would only be needed for NEST, ANNarchy, Brian2CUDA or XyloSim.

4) Install pitfalls:
- lava-nc pins numpy<2 and networkx<=2.8.7; this venv has numpy 2.2.6 and networkx 3.4.2.
- lava-dl pins torch<2.4.
- sinabs and rockpool[xylo] pin nir<=1.0.4; this venv has nir 1.0.8.
- The samna package on PyPI is a stub that runs pip install from SynSense's GitLab index when imported.
- brian2>=2.9 has no cp310 Windows wheel; 2.8.0.4 is the last one.
- GeNN needs Visual Studio Build Tools plus the CUDA toolkit (nvcc).

scout.what_it_models: Lava Processes run on CPU via Loihi1SimCfg/Loihi2SimCfg; ProcessModels in floating-point and fixed-point variants, LIF models tagged 'bit_accurate_loihi' (PyLifModelBitAcc, PyLifResetModelBitAcc, PyLearningLIFModelFixed). Learning-engine widths in magma/core/learning/constants.py: weights 8-bit unsigned (9 signed), traces 7 bits + 8 fractional bits, synaptic-change accumulator 15/16 bits, epoch time 6 bits, tags 8 bits. Models the chip's arithmetic/quantization, not its energy, timing, per-core memory limits or NoC.
scout.learning_support: Yes, programmable local rules in Loihi learning-engine form: LoihiLearningRule / Loihi2FLearningRule / Loihi3FLearningRule take string equations for dw (weight), dd (delay), dt (tag) as product-of-sums over pre/post traces x1,x2,y1-y3 (impulse, tau) plus a third factor (RewardModulatedSTDP), attached to a LearningDense process; tutorials for STDP, custom learning rules and 3-factor R-STDP. No add/remove-synapse (structural plasticity) API seen; pruning would be emulated by zeroing weights (my inference). Prior art built on it: CLP open-sourced in Lava (arXiv 2404.00418) and CLP-SNN on Loihi 2 (arXiv 2511.01553).
scout.cost_model: None on CPU. lava/utils/profiler.py maps only Loihi2HwCfg to Loihi2HWProfiler imported from a proprietary module (loihi2_profiler_api); otherwise it warns 'Currently no profiler is available'. Energy/latency only on real Loihi 2 via the INRC extension.
scout.calibration: Fixed-point models documented as bit-accurate to Loihi hardware; no open energy calibration.
scout.license: BSD-3-Clause (framework) + LGPL-2.1 (lower-level components); Loihi extension proprietary (INRC members only).
scout.last_release_or_commit: lava-nc 0.10.0 on 2024-08-08; last commit 2026-05-13 = README now says 'THIS PROJECT IS ARCHIVED ... All Lava repositories are archived'; Intel announces a new SDK for next-generation Loihi with no date.
scout.windows_native: Yes: lava_nc-0.10.0-py3-none-any.whl, requires_python >=3.10,<3.11; README has Windows PowerShell install steps.
scout.gpu: CPU only. Pins numpy<2.0, networkx<=2.8.7, scipy<2, scikit-learn>=1.5,<2, asteval<0.10 - conflicts with the project venv (numpy 2.2.6, networkx 3.4.2).
scout.install_route_this_pc: Local Windows in a separate Python 3.10 venv (pip install lava-nc==0.10.0); no RunPod. Real Loihi 2 needs INRC membership ('open to all qualified academic, corporate, and government research groups', free) - no individual route stated and the SDK is archived, so the hardware path is effectively closed.
scout.notes: Best used as a constraint checker: if a candidate rule (node perturbation, hub-budget rule) cannot be written as a Loihi 2F/3F product-of-sums with 8-bit weights, it would not run on Loihi as is. Pair with SANA-FE for energy. Frozen dependency set because archived.

scout.name: BrainScaleS-2 (hxtorch / pynn_brainscales via EBRAINS)
scout.family: Analog mixed-signal accelerated neuromorphic chip with synapse-local weight storage and embedded plasticity processors
scout.what_it_models: A physical chip, not an emulator: 512 analog AdEx-capable neurons, 2^17 synapses each with a 6-bit SRAM weight and a 6-bit source address stored locally, 1000-fold accelerated dynamics, two PPUs (SIMD processors) for on-chip plasticity, analog MAC 'hagen' mode (inputs 0..31, weights -63..63) with statistical noise and fixed-pattern deviations, nightly calibration. hxtorch.snn mock=True runs the PyTorch numerical model used for gradients; the tutorial shows it must be manually scaled to match hardware, so it is not a calibrated emulator of analog nonidealities.
scout.learning_support: In-the-loop surrogate-gradient training (hxtorch.snn); local rules as C++ kernels on the PPU (tutorials: rate-coding plasticity, homeostasis dw = sign(nu_target - nu), SuperSpike). Synapse addresses allow 'inserting and removing synaptic connections dynamically'. Structural plasticity with constant fan-in was run on chip (arXiv 1912.12047, Iris 92.3%); reward-modulated STDP Pong (arXiv 1811.03618).
scout.cost_model: Measured on hardware in papers: chip power budget 57 mW in the Pong pilot study (prototype); <200 mW at up to 85k frames/s for surrogate-gradient networks (arXiv 2006.07239). No software energy model in the docs.
scout.calibration: The hardware itself; neurons calibrated nightly.
scout.last_release_or_commit: hxtorch last commit 2026-09-11 (tags ebrains-8.0-a5 from 2024-03-06); docs copyright 2026.
scout.windows_native: No local install: hxtorch builds inside a Singularity/Apptainer container on Linux. Use via the browser on EBRAINS JupyterLab (EBRAINS-experimental kernel).
scout.install_route_this_pc: Remote EBRAINS: free account, Collaboratory with a test quota, more quota via the Job Manager (guidebook dated 2022); EBRAINS says access is free for evaluation and basic research. No RunPod needed.
scout.notes: Closest accessible match to principle 2 (weights stored and applied at the synapse) with on-chip local and structural learning and measured power. Limits: small (512 neurons), 6-bit weights, analog noise; rules must be ported to PPU C++ or hxtorch. Measured energy here comes from a neuromorphic chip, not a GPU; the project rule needs an explicit decision before using it.

scout.name: SANA-FE (sanafe 2.2.9)
scout.family: Architecture-level neuromorphic performance and energy simulator (calibrated)
scout.what_it_models: Time-step-granular execution of a mapped SNN on a chip described in YAML (mesh NoC of tiles; cores with axon_in, synapse, dendrite, soma, axon_out units). Built-in units: current-based synapse, accumulator (with or without delay), multi-tap dendrite, Loihi LIF soma, TrueNorth soma, input. Timing models simple/detailed/cycle (optional Booksim2 NoC). Presets load_loihi() (Loihi 1: 32 tiles x 4 cores, max 1024 neurons per core) and load_truenorth(). Custom hardware units as C++ plugins; Python layers API (Input2D, Conv2D, Dense with numpy weights).
scout.learning_support: None built in (no plasticity or weight-update unit among the models); learning cost would need a custom synapse plugin or post-hoc accounting with a declared, uncalibrated per-update energy.
scout.cost_model: Per-event energy and latency summed per time step; SpikingChip.get_power(). Loihi preset (file comment: SPICE-derived numbers from Davies et al. 2018): synaptic spike processing 35.5 pJ dense / 33.6 pJ sparse / 24.0 pJ conv; neuron update 21.6 pJ; neuron access 51.2 pJ; spike generation 69.3 pJ; message out 111 pJ; NoC hop 3.0-4.2 pJ.
scout.calibration: IEEE TCAD 2025 (doi 10.1109/TCAD.2025.3537971) abstract: calibration methodology applied to Loihi; predicts Loihi energy and latency within 12% and 25% for three real-world applications; TrueNorth model >20x faster than discrete-event TrueNorth simulators.
scout.windows_native: Yes: cp310 win_amd64 wheel (also cp311+).
scout.gpu: CPU (multi-threaded C++); no torch or numpy pin in the core package.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Local Windows: pip install sanafe (main venv or side venv). No RunPod.
scout.notes: Best local option for a scoreboard in a machine's own event costs, consistent with the model-based-estimate rule. Limits: Loihi 1 constants from 2018, inference-side events only; 'learning while inferring' requires an explicitly declared extra cost term.

summary:
Verdict: yes, for the physical-learning branch there is one fast, open simulator that runs on this PC as it is: Rain Neuromorphics' energy-based-learning (Scellier, ICML 2024, arXiv 2402.11674; MIT; plain PyTorch). It solves ideal nonlinear resistor networks (resistors, diodes, sources) exactly and trains them with equilibrium propagation (EP), coupled learning (CpL) or contrastive learning. Its energy function is the circuit's dissipated power, so power per inference and device count come out directly. Reported scale on one A100: DRN-1H (1.6M conductances), 50 EP epochs in about 2 h 36 min. DRN-XL (51.7M), 100 epochs in 10 h 27 min, 1.33% MNIST error. For comparison, a SPICE (Cadence Spectre) run of a 0.16M network took 18 h per epoch.

What must be added as an explicit model:
- equilibration time (node RC, as pyrkm does)
- peripheral and update-circuit energy
- device nonidealities

Calibration sources: the measured transistor CLLN (contrastive local learning network) in PNAS 2024 (10.1073/pnas.2319718121). It reports about 10-20 pJ per edge per inference, about 100 mW per edge for the learning circuitry, and t_h = 100 us, tau0 = 18 ms. Single-cell ngspice-47 runs can fill remaining gaps. All energy stays model-based.

Best chance of an honest positive result: a subtractive self-learning resistor network.
- Train DRN-1H/2H with EP or CpL on MNIST, then Fashion-MNIST.
- Remove edges during learning using physically local signals: edge dissipation dV^2, per-node current budgets (the hub-allocation analogue), or the measurable susceptibility of Guzman et al. (PRX 2025, 10.1103/f2hb-c9s1).
- Add the power term of Stern et al. (APL ML 2024, 10.1063/5.0181382). dP/dk_i = dV_i^2 is a local, activity-weighted decay, the physical counterpart of the weight decay that stabilized node perturbation.
- Score in substrate units (model J per inference and per training sample, device count, settle time) against dense EP/CpL and magnitude pruning at equal accuracy.

Rationale: here a removed edge removes both its dissipation and its per-edge update circuit. On a GPU, unstructured sparsity buys nothing.

Limits:
- Resistor models are MLP/MNIST scale only. CIFAR exists only for Hopfield DCHNs (CIFAR-100, 100 epochs, about 3 h on an A100).
- Elements are ideal, and inputs need large gains (A up to 4000).
- The two-phase training is quasi-static.

Prior art to differentiate:
- tuning by pruning (PRL 2015, 10.1103/physrevlett.114.225501)
- local pruning rules for allosteric networks (PR Materials 2021)
- directed aging (Sci Adv 2019)
- DEEP, sparsity-inducing pruning in EP on tiny tasks (arXiv 2006.08798)
- sparse local EP lattices (arXiv 2601.21945)
- EP/CpL conserve conductance mass (arXiv 2606.15444)
- hardware imperfection drift (arXiv 2505.22887)
- the Restricted Kirchhoff Machine energy scaling (PNAS 2026)
- a diffusing chemical feedback signal as the global medium (arXiv 2203.12098)

This scan found no work that prunes a resistor-network EP/CpL learner and scores it on substrate energy.

Lower priority:
- Photonics: torchonn, L2ight and SimPhony lean on Linux/CUDA. Zeroth-order on-chip learning with power-aware pruning already exists (MixedTrain, arXiv 2012.11148). Optical DFA at about 1B parameters gave only 19.6 vs 26.1 J per sample (arXiv 2409.12965).
- Ising/oscillator EP: OIM-EP on a 784-500-10 net took about 40 h of simulation, with no calibrated costs.
- JAX-MD mechanical networks: CPU-only on Windows and no compute-cost model.
- SPICE: calibration only.

JAX tools are CPU-only on native Windows (the last cp310 jaxlib is 0.6.2). GPU use for them needs the RunPod pod. energy-based-learning, pyrkm and FFzero install natively in the existing Python 3.10 / torch 2.11 venv; FFzero even pins torch 2.11.0+cu128.

scout.name: energy-based-learning (Rain Neuromorphics; fast nonlinear resistive network simulator, ICML 2024)
scout.family: Self-learning electrical (resistive) network simulator / energy-based learning
scout.what_it_models: Ideal-element nonlinear resistive networks: linear resistors (conductances >= 0), ideal diodes, voltage/current sources, inputs doubled and amplified by gain A, excitatory/inhibitory units. Layered 'deep resistive networks' (DRN). The steady state is cast as a QP and solved exactly by block coordinate descent (matrix-vector ops only). Also deep (convolutional) Hopfield networks. No noise, mismatch, finite precision, diode forward drop or leakage. No hardware-calibrated presets.
scout.learning_support: README lists contrastive learning, EP (positive/negative/centered), coupled learning (P/N/C-CpL), truncated BPTT and recurrent BP baselines. Estimators are classes (GradientEstimator -> EquilibriumProp, ContrastiveLearning, Backprop), so a custom local rule plugs in as a new estimator. Pruning: fixing g=0 is physically exact (a removed resistor). Training is two-phase and quasi-static (free/nudged), not concurrent.
scout.cost_model: The energy function IS the power dissipation (DeepResistiveEnergy: 0.5*sum g*(Vi-Vj)^2), so power per free/nudged state can be logged. Device count = number of conductances/diodes. No equilibration-time, DAC/ADC/amplifier or update-circuit energy model; these must be added.
scout.calibration: None. Ideal circuit abstraction; the paper itself notes real diodes deviate (forward drop, reverse leakage, breakdown).
scout.last_release_or_commit: No releases or packaging; last commit 2025-04-06
scout.windows_native: Yes. Pure Python scripts (no compiled code, no setup.py or requirements file). Needs PyTorch, torchvision and TensorBoard, plus PYTHONPATH set to the repo root (README shows bash export).
scout.gpu: PyTorch CUDA. The paper used PyTorch 1.13.1 / torchvision 0.14.1 on one A100. No version pins; torch 2.11+cu128 is untested.
scout.install_route_this_pc: Windows native in the existing Py3.10/torch 2.11 venv: git clone, set PYTHONPATH, add tensorboard if missing. No WSL or RunPod needed for MNIST-scale DRNs.
scout.notes:
Reported runtimes on one A100, batch size 4:
- DRN-1H (1568-1024-10, 1.6M): EP, 50 epochs, about 2 h 36 min (README).
- DRN-XL (32768 hidden, 51.7M): 100 epochs in 10 h 27 min, 1.33% MNIST test error.
- DRN-XS (0.16M): 10 epochs in 0:30 h:mm, vs 1 week in Spectre SPICE (Kendall et al. 2020, 18 h/epoch).
- DCHN on CIFAR-100: 100 epochs about 3 h (EBL README; Hopfield model, not resistive).

The paper claims networks 327x larger trained 160x faster than SPICE.

On the 8 GB GPU, XL weights are about 0.2 GB fp32, so they should fit (my estimate, not measured). The small-batch workload is launch/bandwidth bound; expect the same order of magnitude as the A100 numbers (unmeasured).

Physical caveat: large input gains are needed (A = 4000 for DRN-3H). Recommended primary tool for a substrate scoreboard.

scout.name: pyrkm (Restricted Kirchhoff Machine) + rkm_energy submodule
scout.family: Self-learning resistive network (CLLN) simulator, unsupervised/probabilistic
scout.what_it_models: Two identical bipartite resistor networks (CLLN twin design) whose edges are transistors with gate-voltage-set conductances. Ideal transistors and comparators; injected noise plus comparators implement stochastic binarization (RBM analogue). Gate voltages are clipped to [-10,10] to mimic limited conductance range. Binarized MNIST. The energy analysis adds a constant node capacitance C (RC relaxation).
scout.learning_support: Contrastive local rule (conductance change proportional to the power difference between clamped and free states, PCD-like with twin networks); classification variant; an RBM baseline is included. Source is modifiable; no built-in pruning.
scout.cost_model:
Analytic time/power/energy per operation:
- analog relaxation (RC per node)
- noise generation
- comparator ADC
- gate-voltage updates

Scaling: time per operation O(1) in system size; RKM energy grows linearly with Nh vs about quadratically for matmul. The digital baseline is measured with pyRAPL and nvidia-smi.
scout.calibration: Dimensionless time/power parameters swept (paper Fig. 8). Circuit topology follows the transistor CLLN prototype, but no fabricated-chip calibration of the constants.
scout.windows_native: py3-none-any wheel, Python >= 3.9. Deps: torch (unpinned), torchvision, pandas, scipy, matplotlib.
scout.gpu: PyTorch; the paper trained on an NVIDIA Titan V. Unpinned torch, so torch 2.11 should be acceptable (untested).
scout.install_route_this_pc: pip install pyrkm into the existing venv (Windows native). Use only the analytic RKM cost side: the GPU-measurement scripts (nvidia-smi) conflict with the project rule against GPU energy measurement.
scout.notes:
Best available template for turning a resistor-network simulation into time/power/energy-per-operation estimates (RC relaxation + comparators + update). Pair it with the energy-based-learning solver for supervised DRNs.

The matmul comparison in the paper ran on an i7-13700H + RTX 4050. No training runtime figure was found. Sizes: Nv = 784 visible units; hidden size swept.

scout.learning_support: Coupled learning executed by the hardware itself: twin networks, local updates with no computer in the loop. Q-learning with a contrastive local update in the RL notebooks.
scout.cost_model:
Measured in PNAS 2024:
- about 10-20 pJ per edge for performing learned tasks (from measured voltages/conductances and equilibration time tau_V)
- learning circuitry about 100 mW per edge (can be shut off for inference)
- adjustable timescales t_h = 100 us, tau0 = 18 ms
- control at about 100 kHz
- a 100x speed-up to tau_V about 10 ns projected to give about 100 fJ per edge
scout.calibration: Hardware-measured on a lab prototype (MOSFET edges)
scout.license: Zenodo record: MIT; Dryad dataset license not checked
scout.last_release_or_commit: Zenodo v1.0.1 2025-06-18; PhysicalReinforcementLearning last commit 2026-07-28; PNAS published 2024-07
scout.windows_native: Data files and Jupyter notebooks (Python); the theory notebook needs Mathematica
scout.install_route_this_pc: Download only; use the constants to convert simulated power/time into model-based energy
scout.notes:
Key honest-cost fact: per-edge learning circuitry (about 100 mW) dwarfs inference dissipation (pJ), so energy scales with the number of trainable edges times update time. This is exactly where learning-time pruning pays on this substrate.

The imperfection paper (arXiv 2505.22887) documents a simulation-reality gap: learning bias causes limit cycles and forgetting, absent in ideal simulations. A faithful emulator should inject an update bias.
